content: The Zika virus is a flavivirus primarily transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, with Aedes aegypti being the most efficient vector. These mosquitoes are prevalent in tropical regions, but temperate areas where Aedes mosquitoes are endemic are also at risk for vector transmission. Over half of the global population resides in areas where Aedes mosquitoes are present. In addition to mosquito transmission, Zika virus can spread through sexual contact, blood transfusion, organ transplantation, vertical transmission from mother to fetus, and exposure in laboratory or healthcare settings. Symptoms of Zika virus infection typically appear 3 to 12 days after exposure and last between 2 and 7 days. The clinical presentation resembles other flavivirus infections, such as dengue and chikungunya, and includes fever, rash, conjunctivitis, malaise, muscle and joint pain, and headache. Congenital Zika virus transmission refers to the prenatal vertical transmission of the virus from mother to fetus. This type of infection is associated with an increased risk of complications, including fetal loss, stillbirth, preterm birth, and Congenital Zika Virus Syndrome (CZVS). CZVS is characterized by structural, neurological, and ophthalmological abnormalities. Affected neonates may be born with these abnormalities or develop them within the first month of life. Five features almost exclusively associated with CZVS include severe microcephaly with partial skull collapse, reduced brain tissue with a specific pattern of brain damage (including subcortical calcifications), damage to the back of the eye (e.g., macular scarring and focal retinal pigmentary mottling), congenital contractures (e.g., clubfoot and arthrogryposis), and hypertonia. Infants born to symptomatic mothers with Zika virus are as likely to develop CZVS as those born to asymptomatic mothers. However, symptoms of CZVS tend to be more severe when maternal infection occurs during the first trimester, suggesting that earlier infections in pregnancy are more detrimental to fetal and neonatal development. Among liveborn infants with and without birth defects, 64% and 23%, respectively, exhibit neuroimaging abnormalities. The long-term effects of these abnormalities and their impact on future developmental outcomes remain unclear. Diagnostic testing for Zika virus primarily involves molecular or serological assays. Zika virus RNA has been detected in various bodily fluids and tissues, including blood, urine, cerebrospinal fluid, amniotic fluid, semen, saliva, breast milk, and cervical and vaginal mucus. Two main types of tests are used to determine Zika virus infection: nucleic acid testing (NAT) for detecting viral RNA particles and serological assays for detecting Zika virus antibodies. NAT, such as reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR), detects genetic material and allows for early diagnosis compared to serological assays, which require time for antibodies to develop in the bloodstream. NAT is recommended for symptomatic individuals early in the course of illness and for pregnant women with possible Zika virus exposure. For asymptomatic pregnant women, NAT is recommended three times during pregnancy if there is ongoing exposure. Serological testing detects Zika virus-specific IgM and neutralizing antibodies, which typically develop toward the end of the first week of illness. IgM antibodies can be detected starting four days after symptom onset or exposure and may persist for up to 12 weeks or longer. For symptomatic pregnant women, IgM serology is performed concurrently with NAT. For asymptomatic pregnant women, testing follows a specific algorithm. However, IgM testing is not recommended for asymptomatic nonpregnant individuals. Plaque Reduction Neutralization Testing (PRNT) is used to confirm Zika virus infection in cases with negative NAT results and non-negative serology results. PRNT is considered the reference standard for diagnosing non-congenitally transmitted Zika virus infections but has limitations, including technical difficulty, long turnaround time, and the need for live viral culture. It cannot distinguish between maternal and neonatal infections due to transplacental antibody transfer. Maternal antibodies wane in neonatal serum after about 18 months, so repeating PRNT after this period can confirm or rule out infection. For diagnosing congenital Zika virus infection in neonates, testing is recommended if the neonate presents with symptoms of CZVS at birth, if the mother had a laboratory-confirmed Zika virus infection during pregnancy, or both. Testing should be performed soon after birth due to the short detection window for RT-PCR and waning IgM antibody titers. Cerebrospinal fluid has shown higher sensitivity than blood and urine for diagnostic testing but is only recommended if obtained for other reasons due to the invasive nature of the procedure. Prenatal and postmortem testing is performed on placental tissues, fetal tissues, and amniotic fluid using NAT RT-PCR. Placental testing is recommended for live births of infants with CZVS symptoms, for mothers with unspecified flavivirus infections, and on a case-by-case basis for asymptomatic infants. Testing of fetal tissues is also conducted in cases of pregnancy loss or infant death following live birth. However, testing is not recommended if there is no evidence of maternal Zika virus infection. Treatment for infants with CZVS focuses on monitoring and addressing associated signs and symptoms. There is no cure for congenital Zika virus infection or its complications. However, it is crucial to monitor all infected infants, including those without symptoms at birth, to optimize growth and development by identifying and addressing complications with therapy and a multidisciplinary medical support team. Confirmed cases of congenital Zika virus infection or CZVS require neurodevelopmental evaluations at regular intervals during the first two years of life. The review aims to provide diagnostic accuracy information on available tests to improve the diagnostic pathway and understand the role of laboratory diagnostics for congenital Zika virus. Improving this process will facilitate the rapid management of affected neonates, ensuring optimal growth and development, especially for those who develop symptoms later. This will also contribute to studies aiming to understand the full clinical picture of CZVS.
